claims.text: Engineered multilayer interfaces in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion at engineered multilayer interfaces reduces time-dependent plastic deformation relative to monolithic high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Post-deposition annealing can enhance interface coherence in these multilayer coatings.
Interlayer thickness governs the dislocation-barrier behavior of the multilayer interfaces.
Interface coherence governs the resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Chemical gradients at multilayer interfaces contribute to the proposed structural mediator.
Engineered interfaces act as physical barriers that block or slow dislocation propagation.
Blocking or slowing dislocations delays strain localization.
Multilayer coatings will have lower steady-state creep rates than composition-matched monolithic coatings under identical tests.
Multilayer coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of strain localization relative to monolithic coatings.
The proposed mechanism is effective over approximately 300–1000 K.
A critical interlayer-thickness range on the order of tens of nanometers permits interfacial coherence to be maintained.
Enhanced diffusion along interfaces could affect the measured creep response.
A monolithic coating with the same overall composition and otherwise matched processing is an appropriate baseline for isolating the effect of engineered interfaces.
The hypothesis is falsified if multilayer coatings show neither statistically lower creep rates nor delayed strain localization relative to the monolithic controls.

contradictions.description: The proposed procedure refers to a 'constant-load stress relaxation' test. Conventional stress-relaxation testing holds total strain or displacement approximately constant and measures stress decay, whereas constant load is a creep condition. The controlled variable is therefore internally mischaracterized.
